_README: Bone collagen turnover for the bone (cross-sectional) weaning model: the share of a young animal's bone collagen that is newly made each month, at each age. Values are monthly shares; a yearly turnover T as in WARN (the share replaced in a year) converts as 1 - (1 - min(T, 0.97))^(1/12). In growing animals most new collagen comes from skeletal growth, so the share is high at birth and falls with age. WARN (Tsutaya & Yoneda 2013) estimated these values for human rib bone from tissue-level bone data (included below as 'human', for checking against WARN); no equivalent values are established for livestock. Every livestock table here is a PLACEHOLDER (TBD-LAB): replace it with values from bone growth and remodelling data for the species (e.g. skeletal mass gain with age plus remodelling rate), then set placeholder to false.

tables.label: Cattle bone collagen turnover (placeholder)
tables.source: Placeholder shape, anchored to two benchmarks: bone collagen of young-of-the-year northern fur seals turns over completely in about 8-10 months (Newsome et al. 2006, Marine Mammal Science 22: 556-572), and WARN's human rib values (Tsutaya & Yoneda 2013). With these values about 95% of a newborn's collagen is replaced by 9 months, and turnover slows to a few % per month in adults.
tables.tbd_note: Monthly share of bone collagen newly made at each age in calves and young cattle. Needed from skeletal growth curves (bone mass gain) plus remodelling rates.

tables.label: Human rib collagen (WARN; Tsutaya & Yoneda 2013, Table 1)
tables.source: Tsutaya T, Yoneda M (2013) PLoS ONE 8: e72327, Table 1 ('Collagen (QP)': the share of bone collagen replaced in each year of age, Eq. 9). Each yearly share T becomes the monthly share 1 - (1 - min(T, 0.97))^(1/12), so twelve months replace T (T of 1 or more, meaning complete replacement within the year, is capped at 97%). The first year follows the paper's statement that 96.6% is replaced by 0.6 years (31 weeks): 1 - 0.034^(1/7.2). The quartic printed as Eq. 6 does not reproduce Table 1 beyond about age 2, probably because its coefficients are rounded, so the table is used.
